extracted.intended_audience: new assistant professors / early-career academic researchers applying to NIH/NSF and other funders
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, experience-based guidance for early-career faculty on how often to submit grants, how to balance prelim data vs. number of applications, study section targeting, interactions with PO/SRO, and alternative funding strategies. Emphasis is on surviving the current funding system rather than reforming it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit at least one proposal per NIH standard receipt date
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to have at least one proposal going in to the NIH for each standard receipt date. If you aren’t hitting it at least that hard, before you have a major award, you aren’t trying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author frames this as a minimum effort expectation for new PIs: treat proposing studies as a core job responsibility and keep multiple submission opportunities in the pipeline rather than relying on isolated single attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume the payline odds apply to you
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a look at the payline and assume those odds apply to you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the payline is 10%, expect to submit at least 10 apps to have a fighting chance; apply a 'noob-discount' and consider submitting up to twice that number. This is heuristic planning: no guarantee, but helps set realistic submission volume targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success correlates with submission effort (volume)
rubrics_metrics.description: Success is better correlated with effort (grants out the door) than it is with career rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many successful investigators differ largely in how many applications they submit; pushing more apps increases raw chances. The post and commenters repeatedly argue that sustained, high-volume submission is a practical way to reach funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: One new grant and one revised grant per round is a practical target
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you get rolling, one new grant and one revised grant per round should be doable. They are a month apart and a revision should be way easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the timing of receipt dates to stagger submissions; expect revisions to require less work than a new application. After initial submissions, reuse and adapt text to speed production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base preliminary data on feasibility and reuse across applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Stop whining about preliminary data. Base it on feasibility and work from there. Most figures support at least a half dozen distinct grant applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design preliminary figures to demonstrate feasibility and then leverage the same data across multiple distinct proposals aimed at different aims or study sections. This maximizes the utility of limited pilot results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't wait to resubmit — keep a pipeline of applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn that app around for the next possible date for submission. You’ll have another app to write for the following round, silly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a wait-and-see approach (submit one, wait for result) — instead plan quick revisions/resubmissions and continuous new submissions to keep multiple chances active.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target different study sections / avoid clustering identical submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different study sections should be targeted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting many closely similar applications to the same study section can create negative perceptions ('spray and pray') and may trigger critiques about insufficient response to prior reviewer comments. If multiple submissions are necessary, craft them for different sections or institutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous identical submissions to multiple NIH study sections/institutes are prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not mere bad form it is illegal* under NIH rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not submit essentially the same grant simultaneously to different NIH study sections/institutes. Exceptions exist (e.g., a component of a Center or Program Project may be considered separately), but check rules and consult PO if unsure; if both mechanisms are funded you may have to choose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure application quality — don’t send 'wretched' grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Sending in wretched grants will never get you funded. Or will get you never funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice is conditioned on producing a semi-credible application. 'Don't let perfect be the enemy of good,' but avoid low-quality, sloppy submissions that damage credibility or waste time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance time between generating preliminary data/papers and applying
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocate time between generating more preliminary data/pubs and applying for more grants; publishing demonstrates productivity as an independent investigator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New PIs must publish to show productivity; prioritize manuscripts as needed. Publishing from preliminary data and turning grant intros into reviews are suggested tactics to build a track record concurrent with submitting grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator and Environment criteria matter (as much as Approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formally Investigator and Environment are as important as Approach. Reviewer weighting varies and CV/pedigree can influence outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New investigators may benefit from a 12–18 month window where pedigree and postdoc publications help; beyond that, senior-author papers and demonstrated independence become more important. Be aware reviewers may overweight investigator credentials in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative/higher-probability funding sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize applications for foundation grants or internal institutional funding opportunities (which may have a much higher probability of success) over a long-shot R01.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money is fungible: smaller, higher-probability grants (foundations, DoD, state, institutional) can sustain a lab and may offer better expected value than low-payline federal mechanisms. Consider deadlines and institutional expectations for NIH specifically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call the Program Officer (PO) for general feedback after scoring; do not contact SRO post-review
rubrics_metrics.description: Since you got a score, you were discussed. The PO can tell you some generalities about how it went. And you don’t talk to the SRO post review, generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use PO conversations to get directional input about resubmission strategies and appropriate mechanisms; avoid contacting the SRO after review (unless in the context of a revision where rules permit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be strategic about which idea to submit first given resubmission limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Best advice is to go with your second best idea on the first proposal to gauge the water and certainly don’t use something that you have a ton of preliminary data cause trivialities could sink it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of limits on resubmissions, some commenters advise not burning your strongest idea on an initial submission that might get sunk by minor flaws; use submissions strategically to test the review climate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect variability across study sections regarding required prelim data
rubrics_metrics.description: The need for preliminary data varies by study section. Some R21s or DP2s have been funded with little or no preliminary data if feasibility/proof-of-principle is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate norms of the target study section: some reward big preliminary datasets, others value a strong idea with feasibility. Tailor applications accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden research framing and form collaborations to access more programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Think outside the box to find connections to other programs; collaborations can help expand options for study section/institute assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend talks outside your immediate field and ask whether your capabilities can answer questions others haven't considered. Collaborations and reframing can open more funding venues and reduce dependence on a single study section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reuse and adapt grant text to increase throughput
rubrics_metrics.description: After the first few, you can start taking advantage of cutting and pasting a lot of the grant text together to get a start on the next one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reuse validated text (specific aims, methods descriptions) to speed creation of new proposals. Also suggested: adapt intros into review articles to generate publications from the same intellectual material — but be mindful of quality and journal/editorial concerns about recycling content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be realistic about personal limits and career trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: High-frequency submission advice is only good if you can keep it up while maintaining sanity and meeting personal priorities (family, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals must balance submission aggressiveness with other obligations; some choose to prioritize family or steady smaller grants. Tenure committees may expect NIH submissions, but alternative paths can be defensible depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: New investigator cross-submission special cases (NSF BIO and NIH)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one case known where new investigators without prior federal funding could send a proposal to both NSF and NIH (historically for NSF BIO directorate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules change; verify current policy and consult the PO before attempting simultaneous submissions across agencies. Some commenters recommend confirming with program staff because directorate-specific policies can differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actively request appropriate study section assignment and follow assignment procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Research the study sections and ask for one, by name, in your cover letter. If you don’t get it, call the SRO and ask for a reassignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment processes involve CSR and SROs; proactively requesting the right study section in cover letters and following up can improve reviewer expertise-match. Be aware that POs do not make study section assignments.
